messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla is a 44-year-old prosecutor, a woman who once moved through the world with a sharp, confident stride. That was before the war came to her city. She was not a soldier, just a civilian caught in the crossfire during a period of intense urban conflict. The defining moment happened on a street she had walked a hundred times. A mortar shell landed two blocks away, and in the chaos that followed, she heard a voice—a man’s voice, shouting in Arabic, urgent and close. She never saw his face, but the sound of that voice, the raw panic in it, became seared into her memory. In the weeks that followed, she could not stop replaying it.

Now, that voice haunts her daily. She hears it in the courthouse hallway when a colleague raises their voice in debate, or in the coffee shop when a stranger speaks on their phone. Each time, her body reacts before her mind can catch up. Her heart pounds, her breath goes shallow, and she feels a cold certainty that someone is following her, watching her from a doorway or a parked car. This is not a distant memory; it is a present danger. The trigger—the voice, the feeling of being tracked—immediately pulls her into a state of high alert. She becomes hypervigilant, scanning every face, every shadow, her muscles coiled for flight. She wakes in the middle of the night, her ears straining for the sound of footsteps outside, needing to check that the apartment door is locked, that her husband is still breathing beside her. She has come to believe that safety is an illusion, that it exists only in a very limited number of places: her own bedroom, with the curtains drawn, or the locked bathroom at work.

This constant state of threat has slowly poisoned how Layla sees herself and the world. She used to be a happy person, quick to laugh, confident in her ability to handle a difficult case or a family crisis. Now, she is certain she cannot cope with even the slightest upset. A dropped file, a delayed train, a raised eyebrow from a judge—these feel like catastrophes. She has concluded that the world is fundamentally dangerous, a place where chaos can erupt at any moment, from any direction. What frightens her most is that the vigilance itself seems to summon the danger. The more she scans for threats, the more she finds them. A man walking too close behind her on the sidewalk becomes a pursuer. A sudden noise in the courthouse cafeteria becomes an explosion. Her own watchfulness creates the very triggers she is trying to avoid. She has started to take different routes to work, to eat lunch alone in her office, to avoid any public space where a voice might rise unexpectedly.

The consequences have been concrete and professional. As a prosecutor, she once thrived on the adversarial energy of the courtroom, the quick back-and-forth of cross-examination. Now, she dreads the sound of a witness raising their voice in anger or the judge’s gavel striking the bench. She has begun delegating her most demanding cases to junior colleagues, inventing excuses about needing to focus on paperwork. Her husband has noticed her withdrawal, the way she flinches when he calls her name from another room. She tells him she is just tired, but she is terrified that he will see her as broken, as someone who can no longer handle her own life. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in court last week. A defense attorney, in a routine objection, raised his voice sharply, and Layla froze. For a full ten seconds, she could not speak. She could only hear that voice from the war, and feel the certainty that she was being watched. She excused herself and spent the recess locked in the bathroom, trembling. She is now afraid that she is losing her career, her marriage, and her mind. What she hopes for, more than anything else, is to feel safe in her own skin again, to walk through a hallway without her heart racing, to hear a voice and know it is just a voice.
